title: Move a ball nut from its shipping arbor onto a ball screw
instruction: Move the ball nut from its tube onto the screw, its front end past the red pen line, and put the tube back in its box. Finish with both arms back where they started.
context: Ball screws drive the linear axes of gantry and Cartesian robots, robot seventh axes and robot linear actuators. Builders of these axes buy rolled screws cut to length with machined ends, and the nuts separately, each on the plastic assembly tube it ships on. HIWIN's assembly instructions: put the tube on the screw's end, keep the nut "aligned concentrically and flush with the shaft", slide it to the thread start and screw it on "with a little pressure and a rotating movement"; "The nut must be fully on the thread before the assembly tube is removed." A nut that leaves its tube anywhere but onto the thread spills its balls.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them; heights from the table top. (1) A black granite surface plate, 12 x 18 x 3 in (Standridge B0-12x18x3; any rigid flat block 76 mm thick will do), fixed, from 21.5 to 52 cm forward and from 36 cm right to 9.7 cm left of the centre line. (2) On it, a matched pair of hardened steel V-blocks (124 mm across, 89 mm tall, 70 mm along a 90-degree V 54 mm wide; Penn Tool 57-060-004), their Vs on a line 36 cm forward, spanning 7 to 14 cm and 18.5 to 25.5 cm right of the centre line. (3) Lying loose in them, a HIWIN T7 rolled ball screw, 16 mm with a 10 mm lead (outer 14.7 mm, core 12.5 mm), 400 mm long, 0.43 kg, steel, machined for BK12/BF12 supports: toward the left, a 10 mm journal 11 mm long with a snap-ring groove (its tip 0.1 cm left of the centre line), then the 336 mm thread starting 1 cm right of the centre line, then a 12 mm bearing seat and a 10 mm spigot (53 mm). Its axis is 14.9 cm above the table. A red paint-marker line rings the thread 50 mm from its start. The screw is wiped clean of its preserving grease, leaving a thin oil film. (4) Under the screw's end, a white lint-free cloth folded flat (12 x 11.5 cm) on the plate. (5) The nut's open cardboard box (90 x 82 x 20 mm, grey foam insert) on the plate, centred 47 cm forward, from 1.8 cm right to 6.4 cm left of the centre line. In it lies the HIWIN R16-10K3-FSCDIN ball nut (steel, 0.20 kg; flange 48 x 10 mm with a flat at 40 mm and six 5.5 mm holes on 38 mm; body 28 mm; 45 mm long; 3.175 mm balls) on its white plastic assembly tube (12.3 mm outside, 10.5 mm bore with a chamfered mouth, 55 mm long with a 20 x 3 mm collar at its rear, 3 g). The tube lies parallel to the screw, its open end toward the screw's end (0.6 cm right of the centre line), the nut against the collar with its flange toward the open end, axis 11.6 cm above the table, held level by foam ridges under the flange, the tube's end and the collar. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Balls lost (a rule from the ball size; 0 for good): while any of the nut's ball track lies between the tube and the thread (from the moment the nut reaches the thread start until its rear end passes it), the tube's end more than 3.175 mm (one ball) from the thread start, its axis more than 1.6 mm (half a ball) off the screw's at its end, or tilted over 5 degrees; or the nut pushed more than 4 mm past the tube's open end with no thread there; or the nut screwed back off the thread with no tube butted. Also 0 for good if the screw fell off its V-blocks or the nut fell onto the plate, the cloth or the table. The nut slides along its tube against about 1 N and screws on 10 mm per turn against about 0.04 N m; it catches only once its front end reaches the thread start with the tube's bore over the journal and butted. Otherwise, at the end, on live states: 1.0: the nut's front end at or past the pen line (50 mm onto the thread, its rear end 5 mm past the thread start), the tube off the screw and in its box, the screw lying in both V-blocks, and both arms back where they started (each gripper's fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start); 0.75: the nut at or past the pen line; 0.5: the nut screwed one full turn on (its front end 10 mm past the thread start); 0.25: the nut caught at the thread start with the tube butted; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held 1 s with the screw, the nut and the tube still. In a real trial: count the balls on the cloth (any ball, or a nut that jams or ran off its tube, scores 0); the video shows the tube staying butted while the nut crosses; a ruler from the thread start to the nut's front end, or the pen line, gives its position; the tube must lie in its box; the arms are checked against marks at their start.
reset_notes: Hold the tube's bore over the journal, butted, and unscrew the nut back onto it (HIWIN's procedure for taking a nut off), slide the nut against the collar and lay it in its box. Wipe the screw with white spirit on a lint-free cloth, dry it and lay it back in the V-blocks with its journal tip on the mark. If balls were lost, use a spare nut on its tube.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz). Real sizes and masses; the tube is modelled at 10 g (real 3 g) to keep its joint stable. The tube's fit over the journal is real contact. The balls are not simulated: the thread is a slide joint driven 10 mm per turn of the nut with 0.04 N m stick-slip drag, and ball loss is a rule from the ball size. The nut does not back-drive under an axial push. The flange's flat is not modelled. Cameras 1280x704 (Dream-1: 320x176).
